```{r setup, include=FALSE}
parse_ms_txt <- function(path) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  rows  <- lines[str_detect(lines, "\\|") & !str_detect(lines,"^[+=]+$") &
                 !str_detect(lines, "^\\+[-=+]+\\+$")]
  map_dfr(rows, function(r){
    cells <- str_split(r,"\\|")[[1]] %>% str_trim() %>% .[.!=""]
    if(length(cells)>=2) tibble(term=cells[1], values=list(cells[-1])) else NULL })
}
ev <- function(p,l,c=1){ if(is.null(p)) return(NA_character_)
  row<-p%>%filter(str_detect(term,fixed(l)))
  if(nrow(row)==0||length(row$values[[1]])<c) return(NA_character_)
  str_trim(row$values[[1]][c]) }
fb <- function(a,b) if(is.null(a)||is.na(a)||a=="") b else a
star2 <- function(coef,se){ t<-abs(coef/se); if(t>2.576)"***" else if(t>1.96)"**" else "" }
ci_cell <- function(coef,se){ st<-star2(coef,se)
  lo<-round(coef-1.96*se,3); hi<-round(coef+1.96*se,3)
  paste0(formatC(coef,format="f",digits=3),st,
         "<br><small style='color:#777;font-style:normal'>[",lo,", ",hi,"]</small>") }
```

# I. Background and Literature Review

## A. The zero-dose problem in Nigeria and the Sahel

An estimated 14.3 million children worldwide had received no routine vaccinations in 2024 (WHO/UNICEF, 2024). Sub-Saharan Africa carries the largest share of this burden, accounting for over half of the world’s zero-dose children (GBD 2023 Vaccine Coverage Collaborators, 2025). Nigeria alone holds roughly 2.1 million zero-dose children, the highest number for any single country (WHO/UNICEF, 2024), with the northern states of Kano and Katsina among the most affected (NPHCDA, 2022).

The Sahel, the semi-arid belt stretching from Senegal to Sudan, faces a distinct and compounding set of pressures. Sabahelzain et al. (2025) describe a region marked simultaneously by environmental crisis, including drought, desertification and food insecurity, and by escalating armed conflict, with a wave of military takeovers across Burkina Faso, Mali, Chad, Niger and Sudan since 2021. In 2023, the proportion of zero-dose children in Sudan reached 43 per cent, with Mali at 22 per cent and Chad at 16 per cent (Sabahelzain et al., 2025). Compounding these challenges, vaccination coverage estimates in the region rely heavily on outdated census projections, with the last full census in Sudan and Chad conducted in 2008 and 2009 respectively, and large nomadic, displaced and conflict-affected populations remaining effectively invisible to routine data systems (Sabahelzain et al., 2025).

Distrust in immunisation programmes has its own long history in this region. The boycott of the polio vaccine across several northern Nigerian states, beginning in 2003 and lasting into the following year, was rooted in political tension between the country’s Muslim north and Christian south and amplified by rumours linking vaccination to sterility and HIV transmission. The boycott delayed polio eradication in Nigeria by years and seeded suspicion that persists in various forms today (Jegede, 2007; Ghinai et al., 2013). Sabahelzain et al. (2025) note that the resurgence of armed groups in the same northern Nigerian corridor, alongside similar movements in the Sahel’s tri-border region between Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, creates renewed conditions for vaccine scepticism layered on top of existing access barriers.

## B. DATHARM and the MCHTrack programme

DATHARM, a Nigerian social-technology organisation, developed MCHTrack to address the specific challenge of identifying and following up with zero-dose children across Kano and Katsina. The system uses community health workers equipped with mobile devices to identify unvaccinated children, refer them to facilities, and trace those who default on their vaccination schedule (DATHARM, 2026). Piloted initially in Katsina state in 2019 as a tool for tracking maternal health, MCHTrack was subsequently scaled to cover immunisation tracking across dozens of wards in the highest-burden local government areas (Gavi, 2025). This combination of community-based identification and digital follow-up positions MCHTrack within a broader trend of using mobile registries to strengthen immunisation systems in low-resource settings. The routine, high-frequency programme data it generates remains, to date, analytically unexploited in published research.

## C. Predictors of zero-dose status and tracing effectiveness

The determinants of zero-dose status in sub-Saharan Africa are comparatively well established. A household-level analysis spanning 82 low- and middle-income countries identifies distance to a health facility, maternal education, household wealth and birth order as among the strongest predictors of zero-dose status (Farrenkopf et al., 2023). Spatial studies extend this picture geographically: in Kenya, travel time to the nearest immunising facility was shown to materially reduce the likelihood of full immunisation, with under a third of the population living within an hour’s walk of such a facility under a walking-only scenario (Joseph et al., 2020). In Niger, seasonal variation in this same travel burden, modelled through separate wet- and dry-season cost-distance surfaces, was found to influence vaccination uptake, with the wet season substantially lengthening effective travel times in riverine and low-lying areas (Blanford et al., 2012).

Defaulter tracing and recovery, the second pillar of this thesis, has received comparatively less direct attention in the African literature. The most directly comparable evidence comes from outside Africa. Using a provincial electronic immunisation registry covering 8.8 million children in Sindh, Pakistan, Miraj et al. (2024) found that over ninety per cent of children defaulted on at least one scheduled vaccine, though the great majority were eventually recovered through supplementary outreach. Counterintuitively, children in remote rural areas and those born at home, despite higher overall default rates, were less likely to remain permanently uncovered than children in urban areas or those enrolled through fixed health facilities, a pattern the authors attribute to outreach and catch-up campaigns disproportionately reaching the most marginalised groups (Miraj et al., 2024). This reversal of an otherwise intuitive relationship between deprivation and recovery offers a useful precedent for interpreting comparable reversals within this thesis’s own tracing data.

## D. Weather and health-seeking behaviour

The relationship between weather and vaccination has been studied directly in only a small number of settings, and the picture that emerges is one of disconnected, largely independent inquiry rather than a unified or cumulative body of evidence.

The first systematic test of this relationship in sub-Saharan Africa came from Nagata et al. (2021), who linked Demographic and Health Survey data from 137,379 children across twenty-two countries to thirty-year rainfall records, defining drought as annual precipitation below the fifteenth historical percentile. Drought at birth was associated with small but consistent reductions in BCG, DPT and polio vaccination, with the strongest effects closest in time to the drought itself. The authors note explicitly that, prior to their study, no empirical research had rigorously examined this relationship at all, with the existing evidence limited to anecdotal case reports such as a measles vaccination rate of 47 per cent recorded during the 1983 to 1985 drought in Timbuktu, Mali (Nagata et al., 2021, citing Carnell and Guyon, 1990).

A conceptually related but mechanistically distinct literature addresses climate-induced displacement rather than weather variation itself. Haque, Parr and Muhidin (2019) compared healthcare-seeking behaviour among parents permanently displaced by flooding and riverbank erosion in mainland Bangladesh against otherwise similar non-displaced households, finding that displaced parents were markedly less likely to seek care outside the home for a sick child, and far less likely to use a trained provider when they did seek care, despite their children falling ill more often. The authors are careful to note that their study does not examine climate variability directly, but rather one of its downstream demographic consequences, and that the displaced population’s reduced access to trained providers and higher transport costs, not weather itself, drive the effect (Haque, Parr and Muhidin, 2019).

Outside Africa, the clearest precedent for this thesis’s specific approach, linking high-frequency daily weather to a routine digital health registry, comes from Pakistan. Using over 132 million immunisation records from Sindh’s provincial electronic immunisation registry, Siddiqi et al. (2025) found that heat wave days significantly reduced immunisation delivery, with enhanced outreach activities affected most severely (21.2 per cent decline), routine outreach also substantially affected (13.6 per cent), and fixed-site delivery comparatively insulated (5.8 per cent decline). Rural divisions were disproportionately affected relative to the provincial capital. This is the only published study identified that applies registry-based, high-frequency weather analysis to childhood immunisation anywhere in the world, and it has not, at the time of writing, been extended to any African setting.

A separate and much older literature addresses weather and scheduled healthcare attendance outside the immunisation context entirely, concentrated almost exclusively in high-income settings. Samano et al. (2021) linked thirty years of heat index and precipitation data to an HIV clinic registry in Miami, finding that extreme precipitation increased the relative risk of a missed appointment by thirteen per cent, with extreme heat showing a comparable significant association, using a case-crossover design that controlled for day-of-week effects. The same authors note, however, that theirs was the first published study of its kind, built on their own earlier conference presentations rather than an existing body of comparable work (Samano et al., 2021). The wider literature on missed primary care appointments in the United Kingdom, by contrast, treats weather largely as a self-reported, qualitative reason offered by patients in surveys, rather than as a variable tested quantitatively against objective meteorological data (Parsons, Bryce and Atherton, 2021).

A different population entirely is captured by Fritz (2022), who linked Indonesia’s national health insurance claims to daily district-level meteorological data. The paper found that hot days increased visits for diabetes by up to 29 per cent and for cardiovascular disease by up to 19 per cent, with no comparable effect on respiratory disease. This finding, while methodologically close to the approach taken in this thesis, operates through the opposite causal mechanism: heat here exacerbates an existing chronic condition and increases demand for care, rather than deterring a discretionary preventive visit. Furthermore, the study’s adult, insured, chronic-disease population bears little resemblance to the paediatric, uninsured, routine-immunisation context this thesis examines.

This thesis sits at the intersection of three bodies of evidence reviewed above. The determinants of zero-dose status are well studied across sub-Saharan Africa, but rarely examined through the kind of routine, high-frequency programme data that MCHTrack generates. Defaulter tracing is widely practised, yet its actual effectiveness, as distinct from what is reported, is seldom tested against the underlying records. Weather and health-seeking behaviour have been linked in a handful of disconnected settings, but never in the Sahel, and never against immunisation specifically. MCHTrack offers a chance to address all three gaps from a single dataset, and to ask what such a dataset can and cannot reveal once examined closely.

This thesis therefore asks three questions:

- First, what individual and geographic characteristics predict zero-dose status among children enrolled in MCHTrack, and how does the choice of zero-dose definition bound what those predictors can show.

- Second, what predicts successful recovery through defaulter tracing, and to what extent do programme records support the recovery rates they report.

- Third, whether rainfall, heat and vegetation patterns explain any part of the variation in immunisation-seeking behaviour that the first two questions leave unexplained.

These questions share a common thread. Each asks not only what the data shows, but how far the data itself can be trusted to show it. The chapters that follow take up this thread directly, beginning with the data and methods used to answer each question in turn.

# II. Data and Methods

Answering the first two questions set out above requires individual-level records of enrolment, zero-dose status, and tracing outcomes. Answering the third requires a different kind of outcome altogether, one that varies day to day rather than child by child, matched against weather data sourced independently of MCHTrack. This section sets out both data sources and the modelling choices built around what each can and cannot support.

## A. MCHTrack data structure

Before a child’s record exists in MCHTrack, vaccination in Kano and Katsina ordinarily follows a simpler path. A caregiver becomes aware a child is due a dose, through a community health worker’s house-to-house visit, a reminder from an earlier facility encounter, or word of mouth at a routine gathering, then either travels to a facility or waits for an outreach visit. The dose, once given, is recorded on a paper card kept by the family, the primary record of a child’s vaccination history across most of Nigeria, MCHTrack included.

MCHTrack sits alongside this process rather than replacing it. Community health workers carry tablets and, during house-to-house enumeration, identify children who appear to have missed scheduled doses, entering them as zero-dose in the linelisted dataset at the point of enrolment. A subset are confirmed and logged in the identified zero-dose dataset, which also records the stated reason for non-vaccination where available. Once flagged, a referral is generated, and any subsequent vaccination encounter, fixed-site or outreach, is logged in the facility visits dataset. If a flagged child does not appear there within an expected window, a tracing attempt is triggered and logged in the defaulter tracing dataset, recording contact method, date, and outcome.

```{r fig-2-1, fig.height=4.2, fig.width=8.6, dpi=150}

boxes <- tibble(

  x=c(1,3,5,7))
```

<p class="note">_Four properties of this pipeline bound the analysis. Enumeration undercount (roughly one household in five, per the Kano coordinator) means every zero-dose count is a count of children found, not children who exist. Off-network care is recorded verbally but never verified, which drives the recovery gap examined in Section III.B. Both blind spots are structural, not incidental, and quantifying them is part of the thesis's contribution rather than a caveat to it._</p>

Four properties of this system bear directly on what the analysis below can and cannot show. The first concerns who enters the system at all. Undercounting during household enumeration is a documented problem in Nigerian immunisation planning more broadly. The Kano project coordinator’s own estimate, that roughly one in five households are missed during MCHTrack’s enumeration rounds, sits within this same pattern. No field in MCHTrack records this gap. Every zero-dose count in this thesis is therefore a count of children found, not a count of children who exist.

The second concerns record reliability once a child is in the system. Katsina’s facility visits table showed 38.9 per cent duplicate records and its linelisted table 22.1 per cent, traced to a device handover that caused records to sync more than once. Affected rows were removed before any Katsina-based estimate, and Katsina results throughout rest on a smaller, corrected sample than the raw export size suggests.

```{r fig-2-2, fig.height=3.8, fig.width=8, dpi=150}

dup <- tribble(
  ~state,~table,~dup_pct,
  "Kano","Linelisted",0.0, "Kano","Facility visits",0.0, "Kano","Defaulter tracing",0.0,
  "Katsina","Linelisted",22.1, "Katsina","Facility visits",38.9, "Katsina","Defaulter tracing",0.0
) %>% mutate(table=factor(table,levels=c("Linelisted","Facility visits","Defaulter tracing")))

ggplot(dup, aes(x=table, y=dup_pct, fill=state)) +
  geom_col(position=position_dodge(0.62), width=0.55, alpha=0.92) +
  geom_text(aes(label=paste0(round(dup_pct,1),"%")),
            position=position_dodge(0.62), vjust=-0.4, size=3.1,
            fontface="bold", family="serif") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=pal_state) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,45), labels=label_number(suffix="%"),
                     expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  labs(title="Figure 2.2.  Duplicate record rate by state and MCHTrack table",
       subtitle="Katsina facility visits most severely affected · all duplicates removed before analysis",
       x=NULL, y="Duplicate rows",
       caption="Duplication traced to a device handover causing records to sync more than once. Confirmed by the Katsina coordinator.\nKano is clean across all tables. Katsina estimates rest on a corrected sample smaller than the raw export.") +
  theme_diss(11)

```

<p class="note">Katsina's facility visits table showed 38.9% duplicate records and its linelisted table 22.1%, both traced to a device-handover sync error. Affected rows were removed before any Katsina estimate. This is the reason Katsina results throughout the thesis rest on a smaller corrected sample, and the reason the ward residuals in Figure 3.4 carry a data-quality caveat.</p>

The third concerns recovery specifically. DATHARM’s stated protocol requires a community health worker to physically check a vaccination card before recording a child as recovered, but the defaulter tracing table records only that a card was checked, not which vaccine it showed or when. A successful check simply closes the case. This gap between official verification and verifiable detail is the reason a strict recovery definition and a permissive one that includes self-reported off-network care diverge as widely as they do, taken up directly in Section III.

The fourth concerns geography. A small number of LGAs, Rimi among them, showed signs of backfilled data entered retrospectively rather than at the time of the original encounter. Rimi is excluded from every primary analysis as a result, noted here so its absence from later tables is not mistaken for an oversight.

## B. Geospatial weather data

Weather data is not generated by MCHTrack and is joined to it separately. Daily rainfall is drawn from CHIRPS, a satellite-and-station rainfall product gridded at roughly 5 kilometres and available daily back to 1981. Heat exposure is drawn from ERA5, a reanalysis product combining satellite and ground observations at hourly resolution, aggregated here to daily maximum and mean values. A vegetation greenness index, NDVI, is included as a proxy for agricultural conditions and indirect economic pressure on households, derived from dekadal satellite composites.

All three were selected against the same criteria: daily or near-daily resolution, full coverage of Kano and Katsina across the MCHTrack study period, and a record of prior use in comparable health research. CHIRPS and ERA5-derived heat indices meet this bar most directly, both used in the two studies identified as the closest precedent for this thesis’s approach, an electronic immunisation registry in Sindh, Pakistan and an HIV clinic registry in Miami (Section I.D). NDVI is more exploratory, included on the strength of an established link between vegetation conditions and household agricultural income in Sahelian settings rather than any direct precedent in the immunisation literature itself. Each is matched to MCHTrack’s facility visits data at LGA and day level, the finest resolution at which both sides of the join are reliably available.

## C. Model specification and justification

The data limitations above bear directly on how each research question is answered. This section sets out two model types: a shared logistic regression framework answering the first two questions, and a separate count-based model answering the third.

### i. The zero-dose and recovery models

The first question, what predicts zero-dose status, and the second, what predicts successful recovery through defaulter tracing, are both answered using logistic regression with ward-level fixed effects. The model answering the first is called the zero-dose model and the model answering the second the recovery model throughout this thesis.

Both outcomes are binary, and ordinary linear regression is poorly suited to either, since it can produce probabilities below zero or above one. Logistic regression avoids this by modelling log-odds as a linear function of the predictors. Both models were estimated using feglm() in the fixest package (Bergé, 2018), which fits the same logistic regression as base glm() but absorbs fixed effects computationally.

**Fixed effects. **Nigeria’s administrative structure runs from federal level through thirty-six states, each divided into local government areas, hereafter LGAs, and each LGA further divided into wards, the smallest unit at which MCHTrack records a child’s location. Kano State alone contains 44 LGAs and 484 wards (Bwire et al., 2021), a resolution finer than most household surveys can support, since survey clusters are rarely geocoded below LGA level. It is at this ward level that the zero-dose model and recovery model apply fixed effects, a standard approach in comparable health research wherever the underlying data allows it (Johnson, 2022).

Wards in Kano and Katsina differ systematically in baseline zero-dose rates for reasons unrelated to any individual predictor, including how thoroughly each has been enumerated. Without this, a model risks crediting ward-level differences to distance, the likeliest correlated predictor given how unevenly facilities are distributed. Both the zero-dose model and the recovery model therefore include ward-level fixed effects, giving each ward its own baseline before estimating the effect of distance, age, and the remaining covariates.

This structure also reflects a deliberate move away from an earlier approach. An initial stage of this analysis tested the same predictors against ward and LGA-level zero-dose rates rather than child-level binary outcomes. This was abandoned once the household enumeration gap described above became clear. A rate requires a reliable denominator, the true number of children in a ward, and this cannot be established from MCHTrack alone. Child-level logistic regression removes the need for a denominator entirely, since each child contributes one row and one outcome.

Even so, the enumeration gap leaves one distinction that fixed effects cannot resolve. A ward with an unusually high zero-dose count may have more unvaccinated children, or may simply have been covered by a more diligent health worker who found more of the children who were always there. The zero-dose model cannot separate these two explanations from the records alone, and any ward singled out as a priority for intervention on this basis should be read as a candidate for further field verification, not a confirmed estimate of relative need, a distinction taken up directly when programme implications are discussed in Section V.

**Covariates and ****specification****. **The zero-dose model is specified as:

*logit(P(**ZD = 1)) = β₀ + β₁·Distance + β₂·Age + β₃·Gender + α(ward)*

Distance and age both have strong prior support as predictors of zero-dose status across sub-Saharan Africa (Section I.C). Gender does not, and is included as a standard demographic control.

The recovery model is specified as:

*logit(P(**Recovered = 1)) = β₀ + β₁·Method + β₂·Distance + β₃·Age + β₄·**DaysSinceVisit** + α(ward)*

Of these, only distance carries comparable prior support, and evidence on recovery specifically is thin, with Miraj et al. (2024) the only direct precedent (Section I.C). Distance and age are included because the verification gap above gives reason to expect distance might matter differently once tracing is underway; a child far from a facility may be harder to enumerate in the first place, but recovery can proceed by phone or SMS without travel. Time since the last recorded visit has no precedent in this literature at all, one example of a wider gap in MCHTrack’s current fields returned to in Section V.

### ii. The weather model

The third question, whether weather explains variation the first two models leave unexplained, requires a different outcome. Zero-dose status changes rarely for any child; daily facility visit counts by LGA change constantly, making them the right outcome for testing whether short-term weather predicts care-seeking independent of any child’s fixed characteristics.

The model is specified as:

*ln(**Visits + 1) = β₀ + β₁·Rainfall + β₂·Heat + β₃·NDVI + δ(LGA) + γ(day-of-week) + θ(month-year) + ε*

estimated through feols(), with fixed effects for LGA, day of week, and month-year. The plus-one term avoids taking the log of zero on quiet days, a practical patch that distorts the relationship most on exactly the low-count days most exposed to the gaps described in Section II.A, rather than to weather itself. Section II.D reports the diagnostic used to decide whether a negative binomial model, fitted to the counts directly, is the more defensible alternative.

Siddiqi et al. (2025) and Samano et al. (2021) offer the closest precedent for this approach (Section I.D). Neither registry carries the enumeration or verification gaps documented above, so a null or positive result here cannot be read on the same footing as either comparator, a point returned to in Section IV.

## D. Diagnostic checks

This diagnostic applies specifically to the weather model, since it is the only one of the three with a count rather than binary outcome. The current specification uses log-transformed OLS, chosen for consistency with the feols() machinery and fixed-effects structure shared by the zero-dose and recovery models, and for coefficients that are directly interpretable as approximate percentage changes in visits.

A negative binomial model was tested as an alternative for one specification of the precipitation variable, since visit data shaped by discrete events such as Ramadan closures and market days typically shows variance well above the mean, a pattern the variance-to-mean ratio confirms here and one that Poisson’s equal-variance assumption cannot accommodate. The two approaches agree in direction and significance for this variable, and log-transformed OLS is retained as the primary specification across all three weather variables on the grounds of consistency and interpretability rather than any indication that it performs worse.

```{r fig-2-3, fig.height=3.6, fig.width=7.5, dpi=150}

vm_path <- file.path(era_dir,"06_panel_daily.rds")
if (file.exists(vm_path)) {
  pj <- readRDS(vm_path)
  vm <- pj %>% group_by(lga_clean) %>%
    summarise(Mean=mean(n_visits,na.rm=TRUE), Variance=var(n_visits,na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")
} else {
  vm <- tribble(~lga_clean,~Mean,~Variance, "Gabasawa",31.9,1990.1, "Ungogo",109.9,10751.1)
}
vm <- vm %>% mutate(ratio=round(Variance/Mean,1))
vm_long <- vm %>% pivot_longer(c(Mean,Variance), names_to="stat", values_to="value")

ggplot(vm_long, aes(x=lga_clean, y=value, fill=stat)) +
  geom_col(position=position_dodge(0.6), width=0.5, alpha=0.9) +
  geom_text(data=vm, aes(x=lga_clean, y=Variance, label=paste0("V/M = ",ratio)),
            inherit.aes=FALSE, vjust=-0.5, size=3.2, fontface="bold",
            colour="#333", family="serif") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Mean"="#1D6FA4","Variance"="#C0312D")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=comma, expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.12))) +
  labs(title="Figure 2.3.  Overdispersion in daily facility visit counts",
       subtitle="Variance far exceeds the mean in both LGAs · rules out a standard Poisson specification",
       x=NULL, y="Daily visits",
       caption="Variance-to-mean ratios of 62 (Gabasawa) and 98 (Ungogo) confirm heavy overdispersion. Log-transformed OLS is retained\nfor consistency with the zero-dose and recovery models; a negative binomial check appears in Figure 3.10.") +
  theme_diss(11)

```

<p class="note">Daily visit counts are heavily overdispersed, with variance exceeding the mean by factors of 62 and 98. This rules out Poisson on theoretical grounds and motivates the log-transformed OLS specification used across the weather models. The diagnostic is carried forward to Figure 3.8, where the calendar structure of quiet days is shown to be social rather than environmental.</p>

The distributions of the main outcome and predictor variables, zero-dose rate by ward, distance, age at registration, and raw daily visit counts, were examined before any model was fitted, to confirm no variable behaves in a way that would undermine a linear specification on the log-odds or log-count scale. Distributions showing no notable pattern are reported in Appendix A rather than the main text.

## E. Fieldwork as contextual grounding

Alongside the quantitative analysis, this thesis draws on conversations with DATHARM staff, two field visits to primary healthcare centres in the wider Abuja area, and internal reports shared by DATHARM. This is not an independent qualitative study. No structured protocol was applied and no formal coding carried out. Its purpose is to help interpret the quantitative findings against what people working with the programme observe directly, in the manner of informal colleague commentary rather than a parallel research method, and it is where the household enumeration gap and the off-network verification gap described above first surfaced.

# III. Quantitative Results

## A. Zero-dose model

### i. Descriptive overview

Most children in this dataset live close to a health facility. Distance to the nearest facility is heavily right-skewed, with a median well under a kilometre and a long tail of children living considerably further out. Zero-dose children sit further along that tail than vaccinated children do, though the two distributions overlap substantially, a child can live close to a facility and still be missed. Age at registration tells a related but distinct story. Children enrolled later in MCHTrack’s coverage period are disproportionately represented among the zero-dose group, consistent with the simple mechanical fact that a child identified later has had more time to fall behind the vaccination schedule before anyone notices.

```{r fig-3-1, fig.height=4.2, fig.width=8.4, dpi=150}

ma_path <- file.path(reg_dir,"03_model_a_dataset.rds")
if (file.exists(ma_path)) {
  pm <- readRDS(ma_path) %>% filter(in_primary_sample)
  pm <- pm %>% mutate(zd=if_else(zero_dose_penta==1,"Zero-dose","Vaccinated"),
                      zd=factor(zd,levels=c("Zero-dose","Vaccinated")))
} else { pm <- NULL }

if (!is.null(pm)) {
  pdist <- ggplot(pm %>% filter(hf_distance_km<=5),
                  aes(x=hf_distance_km, fill=zd)) +
    geom_histogram(bins=45, position="identity", alpha=0.6, colour=NA) +
    scale_fill_manual(values=pal_zd) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels=label_number(suffix=" km")) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels=comma) +
    labs(subtitle="A. Distance to health facility", x="Distance (km)", y="Children") +
    theme_diss(11)
  page <- ggplot(pm %>% filter(age_months_at_reg<=60),
                 aes(x=age_months_at_reg, fill=zd)) +
    geom_histogram(bins=40, position="identity", alpha=0.6, colour=NA) +
    scale_fill_manual(values=pal_zd) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels=comma) +
    labs(subtitle="B. Age at registration", x="Age at registration (months)", y=NULL) +
    theme_diss(11)
  (pdist | page) +
    plot_annotation(title="Figure 3.1.  Predictor distributions by zero-dose status",
      subtitle="Primary analytic sample · N = 70,175 · Rimi and GPS-error distances excluded",
      caption="Zero-dose children sit further along the distance tail and skew older at registration, though both distributions overlap\nsubstantially. A child can live close to a facility and still be missed.",
      theme=theme(plot.title=element_text(family="serif",face="bold",size=12.5),
                  plot.subtitle=element_text(family="serif",size=10,colour="#666"),
                  plot.caption=element_text(family="serif",size=9,colour="#888",hjust=0,lineheight=1.1)))
} else {
  ggplot()+annotate("text",x=.5,y=.5,label="Requires 03_model_a_dataset.rds",
    family="serif",size=4,colour="#888")+theme_void()
}

```

<p class="note">Estimates on the log-odds scale; 95% CIs in brackets; ward-clustered SE. Primary definition uses the MCHTrack penta-ZD flag; strict definition requires no vaccine contact of any kind. Under a 95% standard only age at registration is significant in the primary specification. Distance becomes strongly significant under the strict definition, the amplification shown in Figure 3.3. ** p < 0.05 &nbsp; *** p < 0.01</p>

**Table 3.1a.  Zero-dose model — regression summary**

<p class="note">Estimates on the log-odds scale; 95% CIs in brackets; ward-clustered SE. Primary definition uses the MCHTrack penta-ZD flag; strict definition requires no vaccine contact of any kind. Under a 95% standard only age at registration is significant in the primary specification. Distance becomes strongly significant under the strict definition, the amplification shown in Figure 3.3. ** p < 0.05 &nbsp; *** p < 0.01</p>

The analytic sample for this model is smaller than the full enrolled population. Of 89,177 children and adults recorded across both states’ linelisted tables, restricting to children removes 19,261 rows, and a further set is dropped for missing or implausible distance values, including a small number of GPS-error cases where recorded distance exceeded 100 kilometres and was treated as unreliable, and for residence in Rimi LGA, excluded throughout this thesis for the backfill issue described in Section II.A. The resulting primary sample used in the regression below is 73,240 children. This narrowing is not necessarily random. A household enumerated incompletely is plausibly also a household whose distance or location data was recorded incompletely, which would tend to bias the analytic sample toward more thoroughly documented cases rather than a representative cross-section of all enrolled children.

```{r fig-3-2, fig.height=4.4, fig.width=8.4, dpi=150}

wf <- tribble(
  ~step,~label,~n,~type,
  1,"Full linelisted\n(both states)",101312,"start",
  2,"Women\nexcluded",20891,"exclude",
  3,"Missing / implausible\ndistance",2230,"exclude",
  4,"Rimi LGA\n(backfill)",7161,"exclude",
  5,'"Null" LGA\n(unattributed)',1061,"exclude",
  6,"Duplicate\npseudo-IDs",1953,"exclude",
  7,"Primary analytic\nsample",69366,"end"
) %>% mutate(
  remaining=c(101312, 80421, 78191, 71030, 69969, 68016, 69366),
  x=step)
# fix cumulative for display
wf$remaining <- c(101312,
                  101312-20891,
                  101312-20891-2230,
                  101312-20891-2230-7161,
                  101312-20891-2230-7161-1061,
                  101312-20891-2230-7161-1061-1953,
                  69366)

ggplot(wf, aes(x=x)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin=x-0.4, xmax=x+0.4,
                ymin=if_else(type=="exclude",remaining,0),
                ymax=if_else(type=="exclude",remaining+n,remaining),
                fill=type), colour="white", linewidth=0.3) +
  # Start/end bars: white label centred inside (bars are tall enough)
  geom_text(data=~subset(.x, type!="exclude"),
            aes(y=remaining/2, label=comma(n)), size=2.9, fontface="bold",
            colour="white", family="serif") +
  # Excluded bars: dark label ABOVE the bar top, never inside the thin column
  geom_text(data=~subset(.x, type=="exclude"),
            aes(y=remaining+n+2600, label=paste0("\u2212",comma(n))),
            size=2.6, fontface="bold", colour="#C0312D", family="serif") +
  geom_text(aes(y=-4200, label=label), size=2.3, lineheight=0.9,
            colour="#333", family="serif") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("start"="#1D6FA4","exclude"="#C0312D","end"="#1D9E75"),
                    labels=c("start"="Starting N","exclude"="Excluded","end"="Analytic sample"),
                    guide=guide_legend(reverse=TRUE)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=comma, limits=c(-8500,112000)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=NULL) +
  labs(title="Figure 3.2.  Analytic sample construction — zero-dose model",
       subtitle="Primary sample: 69,366 children across 9 LGAs after all exclusions",
       x=NULL, y="Row count",
       caption="Figures from the verified July 2026 pipeline rerun. Exclusions are sequential. This narrowing is not necessarily random:\nincompletely enumerated households are plausibly also those with incomplete distance data, biasing toward better-documented cases.") +
  theme_diss(11) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_blank(), axis.ticks.x=element_blank())

```

<p class="note">Of 101,312 linelisted rows across both states, restricting to children, dropping missing or implausible distances (including GPS-error cases above 100 km), and removing Rimi, the unattributed "Null" LGA, and duplicate registrations leaves a primary sample of 69,366. The narrowing is plausibly non-random in a way that biases toward more thoroughly documented children, a limitation carried into the interpretation of every zero-dose estimate.</p>

### ii. Main results

Distance to the nearest health facility is a significant predictor of zero-dose status in the primary specification (β = 0.043, p = 0.043), consistent with its established role across the literature reviewed in Section I.C. Age at registration is also significant (β = 0.003, p = 0.006), with older children at registration more likely to be zero-dose. Gender shows no effect in any specification (β = 0.035, not significant), a null result that itself contrasts with parts of the DHS-based literature reporting gender effects in northern Nigeria, and may reflect how children come to be enrolled in MCHTrack in the first place rather than the absence of a true effect.

```{r fig-3-3, fig.height=5.4, fig.width=8.4, dpi=150}

coef_a <- tribble(~label,~estimate,~se,
  "Distance to\nhealth facility (km)",0.043,0.023,
  "Age at registration\n(months)",0.003,0.001,
  "Female\n(ref: male)",0.041,0.032) %>%
  mutate(ci_lo=estimate-1.96*se, ci_hi=estimate+1.96*se,
         sig=abs(estimate/se)>1.96, star=map2_chr(estimate,se,star2),
         label=fct_rev(fct_inorder(label)))

pA <- ggplot(coef_a, aes(x=estimate,y=label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0,linetype="dashed",colour="#aaa",linewidth=0.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin=ci_lo,xmax=ci_hi,colour=sig),height=0.15,linewidth=0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(fill=sig),shape=21,size=3.6,stroke=0.8,colour="white") +
  geom_text(aes(x=ci_hi+0.004,label=paste0(formatC(estimate,format="f",digits=3),
            if_else(sig,star," n.s."))),hjust=0,size=3.0,family="serif",colour="#333") +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("TRUE"=col_sig,"FALSE"=col_nonsig),guide="none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"=col_sig,"FALSE"="#d5d5d5"),guide="none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-0.03,0.13),breaks=seq(-0.02,0.08,0.02)) +
  labs(subtitle="A. Primary specification (all predictors)",x="Coefficient (log-odds)",y=NULL) +
  theme_diss(11)+theme(axis.text.y=element_text(lineheight=0.9))

coef_b <- tribble(~definition,~estimate,~se,
  "Primary\n(penta-ZD flag)",0.043,0.023,
  "Strict\n(no vaccine at all)",0.627,0.199) %>%
  mutate(ci_lo=estimate-1.96*se, ci_hi=estimate+1.96*se,
         sig=abs(estimate/se)>1.96, star=map2_chr(estimate,se,star2),
         definition=fct_rev(fct_inorder(definition)))

pB <- ggplot(coef_b, aes(x=estimate,y=definition)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0,linetype="dashed",colour="#aaa",linewidth=0.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin=ci_lo,xmax=ci_hi,colour=sig),height=0.12,linewidth=1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(fill=sig),shape=21,size=4.4,stroke=0.9,colour="white") +
  geom_text(aes(x=ci_hi+0.03,label=paste0("β = ",formatC(estimate,format="f",digits=3),
            if_else(sig,star," n.s."))),hjust=0,size=3.2,family="serif",
            fontface="bold",colour="#333") +
  annotate("text",x=0.34,y=1.62,label="14.6× amplification",size=3.2,
           family="serif",fontface="italic",colour="#666") +
  annotate("segment",x=0.10,xend=0.60,y=1.5,yend=1.5,colour="#888",linewidth=0.4,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(0.12,"cm"),type="closed")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("TRUE"=col_strict,"FALSE"=col_nonsig),guide="none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"=col_strict,"FALSE"="#d5d5d5"),guide="none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-0.05,1.25),breaks=seq(0,1.0,0.25)) +
  labs(subtitle="B. Distance coefficient by zero-dose definition",
       x="Coefficient on distance (log-odds)",y=NULL) +
  theme_diss(11)+theme(axis.text.y=element_text(lineheight=0.9))

(pA/pB) + plot_annotation(
  title="Figure 3.3.  Zero-dose model — primary specification and definitional amplification",
  subtitle="95% confidence intervals · LGA fixed effects · Ward-clustered SE · N = 69,366",
  caption="Panel A: blue = significant at p < 0.05. Panel B: amber = significant at p < 0.01; grey = not significant.\nUnder the primary flag, distance does not reach significance. Under the strict definition it is roughly fourteen times larger.",
  theme=theme(plot.title=element_text(family="serif",face="bold",size=12.5),
              plot.subtitle=element_text(family="serif",size=10,colour="#666"),
              plot.caption=element_text(family="serif",size=9,colour="#888",hjust=0,lineheight=1.1)))

```

<p class="note">Age at registration is the only significant predictor under the primary definition; distance is positive but not significant (95% CI [−0.002, 0.088]). Panel B is the central RQ1 result: restricting the outcome to complete non-contact raises the distance coefficient roughly fourteen-fold. The choice of definition determines what the predictor can reveal.</p>

A robustness check using a stricter definition of zero-dose, no vaccine contact recorded at all rather than a missed first dose specifically, sharpens this picture considerably. Under this stricter definition the distance coefficient rises to 0.598 (p < 0.001), roughly fourteen times larger than in the primary specification. This gap is itself informative. A child who has received some vaccine, perhaps BCG or an early oral dose, but then fallen off the schedule has already demonstrated some capacity to reach a facility at least once, so whatever drives their zero-dose status under the primary definition is more likely timing, a missed appointment, a stockout, a family’s shifting priorities, than distance itself. A child with no recorded contact at all is a cleaner test of pure physical access, and it is here that distance shows its strongest effect. The primary and stricter definitions are best understood as describing two different populations rather than two estimates of the same thing, a distinction worth holding onto when interpreting either number in isolation. A state-by-distance interaction term was also tested and found not significant, so this distance effect does not appear to differ systematically between Kano and Katsina once ward-level differences are accounted for.

### iii. Ward-level residuals: a limit, not a targeting signal

The regression’s ward-level fixed effects can also be examined directly, as residuals showing which wards have more or fewer zero-dose children than the model predicts once distance, age, and gender are accounted for. In Katsina, this exercise identifies several wards with large positive residuals, led by Wagini in Safana LGA at 59.5 percentage points above prediction, Babban Duhu B in the same LGA at 51.5 points, and three further wards across Mani and Funtua LGAs each exceeding 20 points. In Kano, by contrast, the largest residual found, in Maraku ward, Gabasawa LGA, reaches only 13.2 points, and the overall spread across Kano’s wards is markedly flatter.

```{r fig-3-4, fig.height=6.0, fig.width=8.6, dpi=150}

wr_path <- file.path(resid_dir,"04_ward_residuals_classified.csv")
if (file.exists(wr_path)) { wr <- read_csv(wr_path, show_col_types=FALSE) } else {
  wr <- tribble(~state,~lga_name,~facility_ward,~n_children,~zd_observed_pct,~zd_fitted_pct,~residual,
    "Katsina","Safana LGA","Wagini",37,75.7,16.2,59.5,
    "Katsina","Safana LGA","Babban Duhu B",80,67.5,16.0,51.5,
    "Katsina","Mani LGA","Kurfeji",42,88.1,41.3,46.8,
    "Katsina","Funtua LGA","Makera",351,55.3,17.8,37.5,
    "Katsina","Mani LGA","Duwan Makau",41,68.3,40.4,27.9,
    "Katsina","Batagarawa LGA","Bakiyawa",378,54.2,28.9,25.3,
    "Katsina","Katsina LGA","Yamma 2",79,62.0,36.8,25.2,
    "Katsina","Funtua LGA","Maigamji",582,39.2,18.2,21.0,
    "Katsina","Mani LGA","Doro",66,59.1,40.5,18.6,
    "Katsina","Katsina LGA","Yamma 1",64,54.7,36.9,17.8,
    "Katsina","Baure LGA","Hui",149,20.8,3.7,17.1,
    "Kano","Gabasawa LGA","Maraku",89,22.5,9.3,13.2)
}
dup_lgas <- c("Funtua LGA","Mani LGA","Safana LGA","Batagarawa LGA","Katsina LGA","Baure LGA")
wr_top <- wr %>% slice_max(residual,n=12) %>%
  mutate(ward_lab=paste0(facility_ward,"  (",str_remove(lga_name," LGA"),", ",str_sub(state,1,3),")"),
         ward_lab=fct_reorder(ward_lab,residual),
         provisional=state=="Katsina"&lga_name%in%dup_lgas,
         flag_lab=if_else(provisional,"Katsina, duplication-affected list","Not flagged"))

ggplot(wr_top, aes(x=residual,y=ward_lab)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=0,xend=residual,y=ward_lab,yend=ward_lab),colour="#ddd",linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(fill=flag_lab,size=n_children),shape=21,stroke=0.7,colour="white") +
  geom_text(aes(x=residual+1.4,label=paste0("+",formatC(residual,format="f",digits=1)," pp")),
            hjust=0,size=2.9,family="serif",colour="#555") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Katsina, duplication-affected list"="#C0312D","Not flagged"="#1D6FA4")) +
  scale_size_continuous(range=c(2.5,7),guide="none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,72),breaks=seq(0,60,20),labels=label_number(suffix=" pp")) +
  labs(title="Figure 3.4.  Ward-level residuals from the zero-dose model",
       subtitle="Observed minus predicted ZD rate · top 12 wards · dot size = enrolled children",
       x="Residual above model prediction (percentage points)",y=NULL,
       caption="Residuals from the primary specification. Red points fall in Katsina LGAs on the duplication-affected facility list (Fig 2.2)\nand may reflect recording artefacts rather than genuine unmet need. The one Kano ward (Maraku) reaches only +13.2 pp.") +
  theme_diss(11)+theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=9))

```

<p class="note">The largest residuals concentrate almost entirely in Katsina, led by Wagini (+59.5 pp) and Babban Duhu B (+51.5 pp). Most fall in duplication-affected LGAs, so their apparent excess cannot be cleanly separated from recording artefacts. The Kano-Katsina contrast reflects differential data quality at least as much as differential need. These residuals mark where the model and the data break down, not a verified list of highest-need communities.</p>

This contrast should not be read as evidence that Katsina has more genuine pockets of unmet need than Kano. Katsina is also the state where a device handover during data collection produced duplicate records in 38.9 per cent of facility visits, a problem documented in Section II.A and not present in Kano’s exports. A ward whose visit records were inflated or distorted by this duplication could show an artificially large residual having nothing to do with true underlying need. Kano’s flatter spread, meanwhile, may simply reflect that the state’s smaller number of LGAs and more even data quality leave less room for any single ward to stand out, rather than indicating its zero-dose burden is genuinely more uniform. The Gabasawa outlier is a useful test case for this ambiguity. Gabasawa recurs elsewhere in this project’s fieldwork as a ward of interest, and a 13.2 point residual sitting in Kano’s otherwise clean data carries more interpretive weight than any single Katsina figure, precisely because it cannot be dismissed as a duplication artefact. Whether it reflects genuine localised need or some other Kano-specific factor not captured by the model is a question this analysis can raise but not settle.

Taken together, the two states illustrate a limit of ward-level analysis built on routine programme data rather than a usable targeting map. The state with the most visually striking residuals is also the state whose underlying records are least trustworthy at this resolution, and the state whose records are most trustworthy shows too little variation to act on with confidence. Any ward flagged this way is better treated as a candidate for field verification than as a confirmed allocation priority, a point returned to in Section V.

## B. Recovery model

### i. Descriptive overview

Tracing attempts in this dataset are resolved through a small number of contact methods, principally SMS and home visits, and the balance between the two differs sharply by state. Days since the child’s last recorded visit, the clearest available measure of how cold a lead has gone by the time a tracing attempt is made, is similarly skewed, most attempts happen relatively soon after a missed visit, but a meaningful tail stretches out considerably further, and recovered cases cluster more tightly toward the shorter end of this distribution than unrecovered ones do.

```{r fig-3-5, fig.height=5.4, fig.width=8.6, dpi=150}

mb_path <- file.path(reg_dir,"03_model_b_dataset.rds")
if (file.exists(mb_path)) {
  d <- readRDS(mb_path) %>% filter(in_primary_sample, !is.na(method_sms))
  method_out <- d %>% mutate(method=if_else(method_sms==1,"SMS / phone","Home visit"),
    outcome=case_when(tracing_outcome=="yes_ok"~"Confirmed (in-network)",
      tracing_outcome=="yes_off_network_care"~"Off-network (verbal)",TRUE~"Not recovered"),
    outcome=factor(outcome,levels=c("Confirmed (in-network)","Off-network (verbal)","Not recovered"))) %>%
    count(state,method,outcome) %>% group_by(state,method) %>% mutate(pct=n/sum(n)*100) %>% ungroup()
  lag_d <- d %>% filter(!is.na(days_since_visit),days_since_visit<=300) %>%
    mutate(rec=if_else(recovered_strict==1,"Recovered","Not recovered"))
} else {
  method_out <- tribble(~state,~method,~outcome,~pct,
    "Kano","Home visit","Confirmed (in-network)",41.2,"Kano","Home visit","Off-network (verbal)",36.8,"Kano","Home visit","Not recovered",22.0,
    "Kano","SMS / phone","Confirmed (in-network)",35.2,"Kano","SMS / phone","Off-network (verbal)",42.9,"Kano","SMS / phone","Not recovered",21.9,
    "Katsina","Home visit","Confirmed (in-network)",71.5,"Katsina","Home visit","Off-network (verbal)",13.5,"Katsina","Home visit","Not recovered",15.0,
    "Katsina","SMS / phone","Confirmed (in-network)",80.5,"Katsina","SMS / phone","Off-network (verbal)",7.5,"Katsina","SMS / phone","Not recovered",12.0) %>%
    mutate(outcome=factor(outcome,levels=c("Confirmed (in-network)","Off-network (verbal)","Not recovered")))
  lag_d <- NULL
}

pL <- ggplot(method_out, aes(x=method,y=pct,fill=outcome)) +
  geom_col(width=0.62,colour="white",linewidth=0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label=if_else(pct>6,paste0(round(pct),"%"),"")),
            position=position_stack(vjust=0.5),size=2.7,colour="white",
            fontface="bold",family="serif") +

if (!is.null(lag_d)) {
  lag_meds <- lag_d %>% group_by(rec) %>%
    summarise(med=median(days_since_visit,na.rm=TRUE),.groups="drop")
  pR <- ggplot(lag_d, aes(x=days_since_visit,fill=rec)) +
    geom_histogram(bins=38,position="identity",alpha=0.55,colour=NA) +
    geom_vline(data=lag_meds, aes(xintercept=med,colour=rec),

} else {
  pR <- ggplot()+annotate("text",x=.5,y=.5,family="serif",size=3.2,colour="#888",
    label="Panel B requires 03_model_b_dataset.rds\n(median lag: recovered 46 d, not recovered 56 d)")+theme_void()
}

(pL | pR) + plot_layout(widths=c(1.25,1)) +
  plot_annotation(title="Figure 3.5.  Tracing outcomes and timing",
    caption="Panel A: outcomes as share of attempts within each method and state. Panel B: lag-time subset (16,528 records).\nIn Katsina most attempts end in confirmed recovery; in Kano a large share resolve as unverified off-network care.",
```

<p class="note">Outcome: confirmed in-network return (<em>yes_ok</em> only). Log-odds scale, 95% CIs, LGA-clustered SE. SMS contact is the only significant predictor; distance, age, and lag time are null. The lag-time subset is restricted to records with a prior facility visit date and likely over-represents children with prior system contact. ** p < 0.05 &nbsp; *** p < 0.01</p>

**Table 3.1b.  Recovery model — regression summary**

```{r tab-3-1b}

df_b <- tribble(~term,~c3,~c4,
  "SMS / phone contact (ref: home visit)", b1_sms,  b1_sms,
  "Distance to health facility (km)",      b1_dist, b1_dist,
  "Age at tracing (months)",               b1_age,  b1_age,
  "Days since last facility visit",        b1_lag,  b1_lag,
  "<em>N</em>",                            "40,236", b_n,
  "<em>R²</em>",                           "0.117",  b_r2)
df_b %>%
  kbl(col.names=c("","Full sample","Lag-time subset"), align=c("l","r","r"), escape=FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped","hover","condensed","bordered"),
                full_width=TRUE, font_size=13) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" "=1,"Recovery model"=2),
                   background=c("white","#BA7517"), color=c("white","white"), bold=TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(1,width="26em") %>% column_spec(2:3,width="13em") %>%
```
