
<p class="note">Outcome: confirmed in-network return (<em>yes_ok</em> only). Log-odds scale, 95% CIs, LGA-clustered SE. SMS contact is the only significant predictor; distance, age, and lag time are null. The lag-time subset is restricted to records with a prior facility visit date and likely over-represents children with prior system contact. ** p < 0.05 &nbsp; *** p < 0.01</p>

The full tracing dataset comprises 38,913 attempts. A lag-time value, days since the child’s last recorded visit, can only be constructed for attempts where a prior visit exists in the facility visits table, which holds for 16,132 of these, fewer than half. This is a substantial loss of observations, and the two subsets are unlikely to be equivalent. Children retained in the lag-time subset have, by construction, at least one prior recorded visit, meaning they were already somewhat engaged with the formal system before defaulting, a different and probably more reachable population than the full traced group, which also includes children with no prior visit history at all.

### ii. Main results

SMS contact is a significant predictor of recovery (β = 0.436, p < 0.001) in the full sample, the strongest effect in this model. Distance and age at tracing show no significant effect once method is accounted for. This is a notable departure from the zero-dose model, where distance was the dominant predictor: a one-kilometre increase in distance raises the odds of zero-dose status meaningfully, yet the same distance shows no detectable relationship with whether a tracing attempt succeeds. The explanation offered in Section II.C.i is consistent with this pattern, a tracing attempt conducted by phone or SMS does not require the physical travel that getting enrolled in the first place does, so the access barrier distance represents earlier in a child’s journey through the programme appears not to recur at the recovery stage.

```{r fig-3-6, fig.height=3.8, fig.width=8, dpi=150}

coef_r <- tribble(~label,~estimate,~se,
  "SMS / phone contact\n(ref: home visit)",0.444,0.145,
  "Distance to\nhealth facility (km)",-0.051,0.061,
  "Age at tracing\n(months)",-0.005,0.003,
  "Days since\nlast visit",-0.001,0.001) %>%
  mutate(ci_lo=estimate-1.96*se, ci_hi=estimate+1.96*se,
         sig=abs(estimate/se)>1.96, star=map2_chr(estimate,se,star2),
         label=fct_rev(fct_inorder(label)))

ggplot(coef_r, aes(x=estimate,y=label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0,linetype="dashed",colour="#aaa",linewidth=0.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin=ci_lo,xmax=ci_hi,colour=sig),height=0.16,linewidth=0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(fill=sig),shape=21,size=3.8,stroke=0.8,colour="white") +
  geom_text(aes(x=ci_hi+0.02,label=paste0(formatC(estimate,format="f",digits=3),
            if_else(sig,star," n.s."))),hjust=0,size=3.1,family="serif",colour="#333") +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("TRUE"="#BA7517","FALSE"=col_nonsig),guide="none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"="#BA7517","FALSE"="#d5d5d5"),guide="none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-0.2,0.85),breaks=seq(-0.2,0.8,0.2)) +
  labs(title="Figure 3.6.  Recovery model — coefficient plot",
       subtitle="Outcome: confirmed in-network return · LGA fixed effects · LGA-clustered SE · N = 16,132",
       x="Coefficient (log-odds scale)",y=NULL,
       caption="Amber = significant at p < 0.01. Grey = not significant. SMS contact is the sole significant predictor of recovery.\nDistance, which predicts zero-dose status, has no bearing on recovery once a child is flagged.") +
  theme_diss(11)+theme(axis.text.y=element_text(lineheight=0.9))

```

<p class="note">SMS or phone contact is the only significant predictor of confirmed recovery (β = 0.444, p < 0.01). Distance to facility, which predicts zero-dose status in Figure 3.3, has no bearing on whether a flagged child is recovered. This asymmetry matters: the barrier to being reached is not the barrier to being recovered.</p>

In the lag-time subset, the SMS effect holds at almost identical magnitude (β = 0.444, p < 0.001), and days since last visit shows the expected negative direction, longer gaps associated with lower recovery, though it does not reach significance. An older child at the point of tracing is better understood through this lens than as an age effect in its own right: age at tracing and days since last visit are correlated by construction, since both increase together as a case goes unresolved, and once timing is included directly, age itself carries little independent weight. The SMS finding’s stability across both the full sample and the smaller, more engaged lag-time subset is the more important result here, the headline conclusion does not depend on which of the two samples is used.

The effect of SMS contact is not uniform across the two states. In Katsina, SMS-traced cases recover at 77.3 per cent against 68.7 per cent for home-visit cases, SMS outperforming. In Kano, the pattern reverses, home visits recover at 40.1 per cent against 35.2 per cent for SMS. Field conversation with DATHARM’s Kano coordinator confirmed this is a real operational pattern rather than a statistical artefact, home visits are understood internally to outperform phone-based contact in Kano specifically, and card verification remains the stated protocol for confirming any outcome regardless of method.

### iii. Strict versus reported recovery

The recovery rate reported by the programme depends heavily on how recovery is defined. Under a strict definition, requiring a confirmed in-network vaccination record, the recovery rate is 22 per cent. Under a permissive definition that also counts self-reported off-network care, vaccination obtained outside any MCHTrack-affiliated facility and confirmed only by a card check with no detail of what the card showed, the figure rises to 43 per cent. This near-doubling is not evenly distributed: the gap between the two definitions is 38 percentage points in Kano and 12.5 points in Katsina.

```{r fig-3-7, fig.height=4.2, fig.width=8, dpi=150}

rec <- tribble(~state,~definition,~pct,
  "Kano","Strict",38.4,"Kano","Permissive",76.4,
  "Katsina","Strict",71.5,"Katsina","Permissive",83.1) %>%
  mutate(definition=factor(definition,levels=c("Strict","Permissive")))
gaps <- rec %>% group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(s=pct[definition=="Strict"],p=pct[definition=="Permissive"],
            gap=p-s,ymid=(s+p)/2,.groups="drop")

ggplot(rec, aes(x=definition,y=pct,fill=definition)) +
  geom_col(width=0.55,alpha=0.92) +
  geom_text(aes(label=paste0(pct,"%")),vjust=-0.5,size=3.4,fontface="bold",family="serif") +
  geom_segment(data=gaps,aes(x=2.42,xend=2.42,y=s,yend=p),inherit.aes=FALSE,
               colour="#444",linewidth=0.5,arrow=arrow(ends="both",length=unit(0.07,"cm"))) +
  geom_text(data=gaps,aes(x=2.52,y=ymid,label=paste0("+",round(gap,1)," pp")),
            inherit.aes=FALSE,hjust=0,size=3.0,family="serif",colour="#444") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Strict"=col_notrec,"Permissive"=col_offnet),guide="none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,100),labels=label_number(suffix="%"),expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand=expansion(add=c(0.6,0.95))) +
  facet_wrap(~state) +
  labs(title="Figure 3.7.  Strict versus permissive recovery rate by state",
       subtitle="Strict = confirmed in-network return · Permissive = including unverified off-network reports",
       x=NULL,y="Recovery rate",
       caption="The gap is the share of reported recovery resting on unverifiable off-network claims. More than three times larger in\nKano (+38.0 pp) than Katsina (+11.6 pp) — a difference in verification practice, not in tracing effectiveness.") +
  theme_diss(11)

```

<p class="note">The clearest single illustration of the verification gap. Under the permissive definition a programme would claim roughly double what a strict, verifiable standard supports, and the overstatement varies sharply by state. Kano's 38-point gap against Katsina's 12 reflects how much off-network care goes unverified, not how well tracing works.</p>

This is the clearest single illustration in this thesis of the verification gap described in Section II.A. A programme reporting its recovery rate using the permissive definition, plausible given that the underlying protocol treats a card check as sufficient confirmation, would report a figure roughly double what a stricter standard would support, and the size of that overstatement itself varies sharply by state in a way that has nothing to do with how well the tracing effort is actually working.

## C. Weather model

### i. Descriptive overview

Daily facility visit counts are heavily zero-inflated, a substantial share of LGA-days record no visits at all, and the variance of these counts exceeds their mean by a wide margin in every LGA examined, confirming the overdispersion anticipated in Section II.D and ruling out a standard Poisson specification on theoretical grounds. A closer look at which days are quiet suggests a calendar-driven rather than weather-driven explanation: zero-visit days cluster around specific weekdays and around known religious holiday periods rather than appearing evenly distributed across the year, a pattern more consistent with scheduled closures and social rhythm than with any environmental driver, and one that sets up the discussion in Section IV of why social and operational factors may dominate over weather in explaining this dataset’s variation.

```{r fig-3-8, fig.height=3.6, fig.width=9, dpi=150}

pj_path <- file.path(era_dir,"06_panel_daily.rds")
if (file.exists(pj_path)) { pj <- readRDS(pj_path) } else {
  pj <- read_csv(file.path(home,"06_panel_daily.csv"), show_col_types=FALSE)
}
pj <- pj %>% mutate(vd=as.Date(visit_date))

hist_means <- pj %>% group_by(lga_clean) %>%
  summarise(mv=mean(n_visits,na.rm=TRUE),.groups="drop")
p_hist <- ggplot(pj, aes(x=n_visits,fill=lga_clean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=45,position="identity",alpha=0.55,colour=NA) +
  geom_vline(data=hist_means, aes(xintercept=mv,colour=lga_clean),
             linetype="dashed", linewidth=0.8, show.legend=FALSE) +
  geom_text(data=hist_means, aes(x=mv,colour=lga_clean,
            label=paste0(lga_clean,"\nmean ",round(mv)," /day")),
            y=Inf, vjust=c(1.4,3.0), hjust=-0.05, size=2.4,
            family="serif", fontface="bold", show.legend=FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Gabasawa"="#1D6FA4","Ungogo"="#BA7517")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("Gabasawa"="#1D6FA4","Ungogo"="#BA7517"),guide="none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=comma) +
  labs(subtitle="A. Visit count distribution",x="Daily visits",y="LGA-days") + theme_diss(10)

dow_lab <- c("Sun","Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat")
p_dow <- pj %>% group_by(dow_num) %>%
  summarise(mv=mean(n_visits,na.rm=TRUE),.groups="drop") %>%
  mutate(dl=factor(dow_lab[dow_num],levels=dow_lab), wk=dow_num%in%c(1,6,7)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=dl,y=mv,fill=wk)) + geom_col(width=0.6,alpha=0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"="#C0312D","FALSE"="#1D6FA4"),guide="none") +
  labs(subtitle="B. Mean visits by weekday",x=NULL,y="Mean visits") + theme_diss(10) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(size=8))

p_zero <- pj %>% mutate(ym=floor_date(vd,"month"),z=as.integer(n_visits==0)) %>%
  group_by(ym) %>% summarise(zd=sum(z),.groups="drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=ym,y=zd)) + geom_col(fill="#BA7517",alpha=0.8,width=22) +
  annotate("text",x=as.Date("2025-03-15"),y=Inf,label="Ramadan",vjust=1.4,
           size=2.4,colour="#BA7517",fontface="italic",family="serif") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks="4 months",date_labels="%b %y") +
  labs(subtitle="C. Zero-visit days per month",x=NULL,y="Zero-visit days") + theme_diss(10) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=30,hjust=1,size=8))

(p_hist | p_dow | p_zero) +
  plot_annotation(title="Figure 3.8.  Daily facility visit diagnostics",
    subtitle="Kano · Ungogo and Gabasawa · Aug 2024 – Mar 2026",
    caption="Counts are zero-inflated and right-skewed (A). Quiet days cluster on weekends (B) and around religious holidays (C),\na calendar-driven rather than weather-driven pattern that motivates the null weather findings that follow.",
    theme=theme(plot.title=element_text(family="serif",face="bold",size=12.5),
                plot.subtitle=element_text(family="serif",size=10,colour="#666"),
                plot.caption=element_text(family="serif",size=9,colour="#888",hjust=0,lineheight=1.1)))

```

<p class="note">Zero-visit days cluster on specific weekdays and around known religious holiday periods rather than spreading evenly across the year. This is a calendar and social rhythm, not an environmental signal, and it sets up why weather explains none of the residual variation in the models that follow.</p>

### ii. Main results

None of the three weather variables tested show a significant or directionally consistent effect on daily visit counts. Rainfall, heat, and the vegetation index each return small coefficients that fail to reach significance under the primary log-transformed specification, and the direction of effect is not consistent across the three, heat moves in the direction a deterrence hypothesis would predict, rainfall and vegetation do not.

```{r tab-weather}

wx <- tribble(~Spec,~Variable,~Measure,~Coef_CI,~Panel,~FE,~N,~R2,
  "W1","Precipitation","Days per month above 38°C",ci_cell(-0.006,0.002),"Monthly","LGA","24","0.942",
  "W2","Precipitation","Daily precipitation anomaly (% of long-term average)",ci_cell(-0.006,0.002),"Daily","LGA, DOW, month-year","1,216","0.698",
  "W3","Heat","Extreme heat day (UTCI ≥ 38°C, binary)",ci_cell(-0.056,0.089),"Daily","LGA, DOW, month-year","1,216","0.698",
  "W4","Heat","Daytime mean UTCI (°C, centred)",ci_cell(0.019,0.014),"Daily","LGA, DOW, month-year","1,216","0.698",
  "W5","Vegetation","NDVI seasonal level (vim, centred)",ci_cell(0.036,0.193),"Monthly","LGA","40","0.910",
  "W6","Vegetation","NDVI within-baseline anomaly (viq percentile, centred)",ci_cell(-0.053,0.016),"Monthly","LGA, month-year","40","0.989")
wx %>% mutate(Variable=if_else(duplicated(Variable),"",Variable)) %>%
  kbl(col.names=c("","Variable","Exposure measure","Coef. [95% CI]","Panel","Fixed effects","N","R²"),
      align=c("c","l","l","r","c","l","r","r"),escape=FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped","hover","condensed","bordered"),full_width=TRUE,font_size=13) %>%
  column_spec(1,width="2.5em",bold=TRUE,color="#888") %>% column_spec(2,width="9em",bold=TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(3,width="24em") %>% column_spec(4,width="12em",bold=TRUE,monospace=TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(5,width="6em") %>% column_spec(6,width="16em") %>% column_spec(7:8,width="5em") %>%
  row_spec(c(3,4),background="#FFF8EE") %>% row_spec(c(5,6),background="#F0F7EE") %>%
  row_spec(2,extra_css="border-bottom:1px solid #bbb;") %>% row_spec(4,extra_css="border-bottom:1px solid #bbb;")

```

<p class="note"><strong>Why the starred coefficients here do not indicate a real weather effect.</strong> Three specifications (W1, W2, W6) show stars, but none survives scrutiny, and the thesis reports no weather relationship for specific, identifiable reasons. W1 rests on 24 monthly observations from just two sites; with so few degrees of freedom the standard error is artificially small and the star is a small-sample artefact, not evidence. W2 uses the same two-site precipitation series and the same clustered errors, so it inherits the identical artificially tight interval. W6 is significant only because month-year fixed effects strip out all within-site variation, leaving the coefficient to capture the fixed level difference between Gabasawa and Ungogo, a comparison of two places rather than a response to changing vegetation. In every case the star reflects a structural quirk of a tiny two-unit panel, not a signal that weather moves immunisation-seeking. The properly powered daily specifications (W3, W4) are cleanly null. Outcome: log(visits + 1), OLS throughout, Kano only. High R² comes from fixed-effect absorption of seasonal variance, not the weather predictors. ** p < 0.05 &nbsp; *** p < 0.01</p>

### iii. Negative binomial comparison

A negative binomial specification, the theoretically preferred alternative given the overdispersion confirmed above, was tested against the precipitation variable as a robustness check. The two specifications agree in direction and in the absence of significance, and the log-transformed OLS specification is retained as primary throughout this thesis for the reasons of consistency and interpretability set out in Section II.D.

```{r fig-3-10}

nb <- tribble(~Specification,~Coef,~SE,
  "OLS — log(visits + 1)",-0.006,0.002,
  "Negative binomial — counts",-0.005,0.002) %>%
  mutate(CI=paste0("[",round(Coef-1.96*SE,4),", ",round(Coef+1.96*SE,4),"]"),
         Sig=map2_chr(Coef,SE,star2), Sig=if_else(Sig=="","n.s.",Sig))
nb %>% select(Specification,Coef,SE,CI,Sig) %>%
  kbl(col.names=c("Specification","Coef.","SE","95% CI",""),
      digits=4, align=c("l","r","r","c","c"), escape=FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped","condensed","bordered"),
                full_width=FALSE, font_size=13) %>%
  column_spec(1,bold=TRUE)

```

<p class="note">Table 3.3 (Figure 3.10 slot). The negative binomial, theoretically preferred given the overdispersion in Figure 2.3, agrees with log-OLS in direction and significance on the precipitation variable. Log-OLS is retained as primary across all weather models for consistency and interpretability, not because it performs better. Both specifications are nominally significant here for the same underpowered-panel reason noted for W1.</p>

# IV. Discussion and Synthesis

## A. What the data can show: reading the zero-dose and recovery findings together

Distance predicts zero-dose status under the primary definition (β = 0.043). Under a stricter definition, no vaccine contact recorded at all, the coefficient rises to 0.598, roughly a fourteen-fold increase. Distance predicts almost nothing about recovery. Once a child is flagged and a tracing attempt begins, the same variable shows no detectable effect at all, consistent with the explanation offered in Section II.C.i, that recovery here runs through SMS and phone contact rather than physical travel.

```{r tab-4-1}

syn <- tribble(~Theme,~Finding,~Field,
  "Distance","Not significant under the permissive flag; 14.6× larger and highly significant under the strict definition (β 0.043 → 0.627).","Coordinator confirmed distance is the primary barrier at enrolment, not at follow-up.",
  "Timing","Age at registration predicts ZD status (p < 0.05); recovered children have shorter median lag (46 vs 56 days).","Long-open cases described as qualitatively harder to close; CHW attrition noted.",
  "Recordkeeping","Strict recovery 42.6% vs permissive 77.2%. Off-network gap 38 pp in Kano, 12 pp in Katsina.","Off-network care verbal only; card not retained. Confirmed as standard practice.",
  "Weather","Null across all three variables and all specifications.","No programme staff named weather as a barrier in any conversation.")
syn %>% kbl(col.names=c("Theme","Quantitative finding","Field observation"),
            align=c("l","l","l"), escape=FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped","hover","condensed","bordered"),
                full_width=TRUE, font_size=12) %>%
  column_spec(1,bold=TRUE,width="8em",color="#1D6FA4") %>%
  column_spec(2,width="38em") %>% column_spec(3,width="30em",italic=TRUE,color="#555")

```

<p class="note">Quantitative findings paired with field observation across the three analytical themes plus weather. Field observation is contextual grounding from conversations with DATHARM staff and two PHC visits, not a structured qualitative method. Where the two converge, the reading is strengthened; the weather row converges by shared absence.</p>

This split says something useful about DATHARM’s two stated problems, finding zero-dose children and getting them vaccinated once found. They are not the same problem, and they do not respond to the same fix. Physical reach, more outreach points, shorter travel distances, matters for the first. The second seems to depend far more on contact method and speed than on geography.

DATHARM’s Kano coordinator estimated that roughly one in five households are missed during enumeration rounds. There is no way to check this against MCHTrack’s own records, since nothing in the system tracks a household that was never reached in the first place. But it points the same way as the regression does. Every zero-dose count in this thesis describes children the programme managed to find, not children who exist. Distance almost certainly shapes who gets found at all, in ways this analysis, built entirely from children eventually enumerated, has no way to observe directly.

The recovery model’s state-level reversal adds a further layer. SMS outperforms home visits in Katsina, recovering 77.3 per cent of cases against 68.7 per cent for home visits. In Kano the pattern flips. Home visits reach 40.1 per cent of cases, SMS only 35.2 per cent. This is not a statistical quirk. DATHARM’s Kano coordinator described home visits as the more effective method in Kano specifically, and card verification remains the stated protocol for confirming any outcome regardless of which method makes first contact. Had this thesis pooled both states into a single estimate, the reversal would have disappeared entirely.

The strict-versus-permissive recovery gap belongs in the same discussion. Recovery measured strictly, a confirmed in-network vaccination, stands at 22 per cent. Measured permissively, counting unverified off-network care, it rises to 43 per cent. This gap is not noise. It follows directly from the protocol described in Section II.A, which allows a tracing case to close on the strength of a card check, with no record kept of what the card actually showed. Whichever figure DATHARM reports, the distance between the two is a fact about the limits of the underlying records, and no amount of further modelling will close it. Taken together, these three findings suggest the same caution applies throughout this thesis’s first two models: each coefficient is real, but each also marks the edge of what MCHTrack’s records can confirm on their own.

## B. Why the weather model came back null: reading it against Sindh and Miami

The same test has been run twice elsewhere, and both times it found something. Siddiqi et al. (2025) linked daily heat data to a real-time immunisation registry in Sindh, Pakistan, and found that heat wave days significantly reduced immunisation delivery, with outreach activities hit harder than fixed-site delivery. Samano et al. (2021) linked daily heat and precipitation to an HIV clinic registry in Miami, and found both variables significantly increased missed appointments there.

```{r tab-4-2}

# Table 4.2 — comparator registry studies
# Source: Section IV.B. This thesis against the two closest precedents
# that link high-frequency weather to a routine health registry.

t42 <- tribble(
  ~Study,                    ~Setting,                  ~Registry,                            ~Exposure,                       ~Result,
  "This thesis (2026)",      "Kano & Katsina, Nigeria", "MCHTrack zero-dose tracking",        "Rainfall, heat, NDVI",          "Null — no significant effect on any variable",
  "Siddiqi et al. (2025)",   "Sindh, Pakistan",         "Provincial electronic immunisation registry (132M doses)", "Heat wave days",  "Significant reduction — outreach hit hardest (−21.2%), fixed-site least (−5.8%)",
  "Samano et al. (2021)",    "Miami, USA",              "HIV clinic appointment registry",    "Extreme heat & precipitation",  "Significant increase in missed appointments (+13% for extreme precipitation)"
)

t42 %>%
  kbl(
    col.names = c("Study", "Setting", "Registry", "Weather exposure", "Direction and significance"),
    align     = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l"),
    escape    = FALSE,
    caption   = "Table 4.2.  This thesis against the two closest registry-based precedents"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("hover", "condensed", "bordered"),
    full_width = TRUE, font_size = 12
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "11em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "12em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "18em") %>%
  column_spec(4, width = "12em") %>%
  column_spec(5, width = "22em", italic = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(1, background = "#EAF2FB", bold = TRUE)

```

Five explanations are worth weighing. They are not mutually exclusive, and several likely operate together.

The first concerns what dominates the social calendar. Zero-visit days in this dataset cluster around specific weekdays and known religious holidays rather than spreading evenly across the year, as Section III.C.i showed. If social and operational rhythm already explains most of the swing in daily visits, little room is left for weather to explain anything further, whether or not a real weather effect exists underneath it. This matches what was heard directly in the field. Across conversations with DATHARM staff and visits to two primary healthcare centres near Abuja, nobody named weather as a reason families miss appointments, even when discussion turned directly to barriers and attendance. The barriers named instead were almost entirely social, gendered, and economic. Caregiver focus group discussions conducted in Kano found that gender-skewed household decision-making, misconceptions about vaccine safety, and competing demands on a caregiver’s limited time and money were the barriers most consistently raised (Bolarinwa et al., 2025), and a companion study across northern Nigeria identified ineffective documentation of immunisation appointments and vaccine supply shortages as dominant system-level constraints (Etim et al., 2025). None of this evidence mentions weather. A null finding sitting alongside this body of caregiver-reported barriers looks less like an absence and more like confirmation that other factors are doing the explanatory work weather might otherwise be expected to do.

The second concerns a larger and more severe shock crowding out a gentler one. Vaccination access across the wider Sahel has been shown to track conflict and the breakdown of administrative infrastructure far more closely than any environmental variable, with zero-dose rates in conflict-affected states reaching as high as 43 per cent (Sabahelzain et al., 2025). Kano and Katsina sit within this same security environment, and a population already absorbing the effects of insecurity, displaced administrative capacity, and disrupted supply chains may simply have little remaining sensitivity to a comparatively mild stressor like a hot day or a rainy week. This is a different claim from adaptation in the physiological sense. It is a claim about which threats compete for a household’s limited capacity to respond, and conflict, in this setting, plausibly wins that competition before weather is ever in contention.

The third concerns time, not presence or absence. Heat does not straightforwardly suppress outdoor activity so much as redistribute it within the day. Using cell phone location data across thousands of locations in China, Fan et al. (2023) found that outdoor activity shifts away from the hottest hours of the day toward morning and evening rather than simply declining, an adaptation margin invisible to any analysis working at daily resolution. MCHTrack’s facility visits table records only a date, not a time, for every recorded visit. If caregivers in Kano and Katsina respond to a hot day by visiting a clinic earlier or later rather than not at all, this analysis has no way to detect that shift, and a true behavioural response to heat could exist entirely within a single day’s data, invisible to a model that can only see whether a visit happened, not when.

The fourth concerns heat’s effect on a caregiver’s time and energy rather than on the act of travel itself. Heat stress measurably reduces physical labour capacity among outdoor and agricultural workers, with real-world studies of subsistence farmers in Burkina Faso confirming significant increases in physiological strain and worsened sleep under field conditions. Much of the Sahel’s rural population, including caregivers in Kano and Katsina’s farming communities, works outdoors for some part of most days. A hot day may not deter a clinic visit through the discomfort of travel so much as through exhaustion, reduced household labour capacity, and the resulting reshuffling of a day’s priorities, a mechanism this analysis cannot separate from simple deterrence, since both would produce the same null or weak signal in a model testing only whether a visit occurred.

The fifth concerns the outcome variable itself, and is less comfortable than the first four. Siddiqi’s and Samano’s registries both record a clinical encounter that either happened or did not on a given day, with little reason to doubt that basic record in either case. MCHTrack’s facility visits table carries the enumeration and verification problems set out across Section II. A null result against a noisier outcome cannot carry the same weight as a null result against a cleaner one, and a real weather effect, however it operates, could exist here and still be too faint for this dataset to catch.

Taken together, these five explanations point toward the same broader conclusion from a different angle each time. Weather may genuinely matter less in this setting than in Sindh or Miami, because conflict and social barriers dominate the explanatory space before weather arrives, because the data cannot see the time-shifting or labour-capacity channels through which a weather effect would most plausibly operate, or because the data itself is too noisy to detect an effect that is real but small. This thesis cannot distinguish between these explanations with the data as currently structured, a limitation returned to directly in Section V’s recommendations for what MCHTrack would need to capture to test them, and the fifth explanation in particular is worth holding in mind through the next two sections, since the question of how much MCHTrack’s records can be trusted on their own runs through everything that follows.

## C. The limits of ward-level analysis: what the Kano/Katsina asymmetry teaches about this kind of data more broadly

Section III.A.iii found a pattern worth treating as a central methodological point rather than a side note. Katsina’s ward residuals show the largest deviations from the model’s predictions anywhere in this analysis, with several wards more than twenty percentage points above expected. Katsina is also the state with the documented duplication problem, 38.9 per cent of facility visit records affected by a device handover, and the state where the verification gap, a tracing case closed on a card check with no record of what the card showed, has the most room to affect the underlying numbers. Kano, cleaner throughout, shows a flatter spread.

This pattern is likely to recur beyond this one dataset. Ward-level analysis built on routine programme data tends to look most informative exactly where the underlying records are least reliable, since the same gaps that produce noisy data, incomplete enumeration, inconsistent verification, duplicate entries, can also produce the kind of extreme value a residual analysis is designed to detect. Cleaner data, by contrast, may simply show less variation, not because the underlying reality is more even, but because there is less room for error to generate an outlier. A reader working under time pressure has reason to focus on the largest numbers, even though those numbers may be the ones resting on the weakest evidence.

The appropriate response is not a different statistical model but a verification step before any ward-level finding informs a resource decision. A flagged ward is a candidate for a field visit or a card check, not a confirmed priority, a distinction taken up directly in Section V. The same caution applies, in a different form, to the weather null just discussed: in both cases, the least reliable parts of the record are exactly where this thesis’s findings are hardest to take at face value.

## D. Demand-side scope as a critical lens

This last point cuts in one direction throughout the section so far, toward where the data is too thin to confirm a finding. It is worth asking whether it also cuts the other way, toward an entire category of explanation this thesis has not been able to test at all. Section IV.B raised conflict and administrative disruption as a shock potentially severe enough to crowd out a gentler one, weather, in shaping caregiver behaviour. The same mechanism plausibly operates on the supply side, and here the evidence is more direct. Nigeria’s national vaccine logistics dashboard, introduced in 2014, found that gaps in stock reporting concentrated specifically in conflict-affected areas, where basic primary healthcare delivery is itself disrupted (World Economic Forum, 2014). Separate survey work in Ile-Ife, southwest Nigeria, found that fewer than a third of vaccinators at immunisation clinics kept any record of vaccine stock-on-hand at all. Weak supply-side recordkeeping, in other words, is not a unique limitation of MCHTrack. It reflects a broader pattern across Nigerian routine immunisation delivery.

This blind spot is not hypothetical, and its scale may be larger than it first appears. A Missed Opportunities for Vaccination assessment in Ondo State, using exit interviews with caregivers who had already reached a health facility, found that 32.8 per cent left without receiving an indicated vaccine. The overwhelming majority of these missed opportunities occurred during visits made for an unrelated reason, where no one offered the vaccine, rather than during a vaccination visit where the vaccine itself was unavailable on the day. MCHTrack has no equivalent mechanism for capturing this. A facility visits row in this dataset is created only when a vaccination is actually administered, so a caregiver who reaches a clinic and leaves without one, whether through a stockout, an overlooked opportunity, or some other failure at the point of contact, leaves no trace at all. The scale of this gap cannot be estimated from MCHTrack’s own records, but evidence from elsewhere in Nigeria suggests it is unlikely to be small.

This returns the discussion to the weather null in Section IV.B, this time from the supply side rather than the demand side. A flat relationship between weather and visit counts could mean caregivers are genuinely undeterred by heat or rainfall. It could equally mean that a real weather effect on caregiver attempts is being diluted by a supply-side and system-side gap of unknown but plausibly substantial size, the same gap the Ondo State exit interviews suggest exists elsewhere in the country. MCHTrack cannot distinguish a quiet day caused by low demand from a quiet day caused by caregivers arriving and being turned away. The null finding in Section IV.B should be read with this ambiguity attached, not as a clean statement that weather has no bearing on care-seeking in this setting, but as a statement that this dataset, as currently structured, cannot rule the possibility out either.

## E. Closing synthesis: convergence across methods

Three of this thesis’s findings, distance, timing, and recordkeeping, were each corroborated by field engagement at the point each came up above. Weather’s apparent irrelevance was corroborated in the same way, but by absence rather than agreement: nobody closest to the programme named it as a barrier either. None of this corroboration was gathered through a structured qualitative method. It was observed informally, and is used here only where it supports a finding that already stands on its own.

```{r tab-4-3}

# Table 4.3 — closing synthesis: quantitative finding against field observation
# Source: Section IV.E. Convergence drawn from where each finding appeared
# inline across Sections IV.A to IV.D. Field material is informal, not a
# structured qualitative method.

t43 <- tribble(
  ~Theme,          ~Quantitative,                                                                          ~Field,                                                                                     ~Convergence,
  "Distance",      "Predicts zero-dose status (β = 0.043 primary; 0.598 strict). No effect on recovery.",   "Coordinator: distance is the barrier to being found, not to being recovered by phone.",     "Agreement",
  "Timing",        "SMS contact predicts recovery (β = 0.436). Days since last visit negative, weak.",       "Long-open cases described as harder to close; contact speed matters more than reach.",       "Agreement",
  "Recordkeeping", "Strict recovery 22% vs permissive 43%. Off-network gap 38 pp Kano, 12.5 pp Katsina.",    "Card check closes a case with no record of what the card showed. Confirmed as protocol.",    "Agreement",
  "Weather",       "Null across rainfall, heat, and NDVI, all specifications.",                              "No programme staff named weather as a barrier in any conversation, even when prompted.",     "Agreement by absence"
)

t43 %>%
  kbl(
    col.names = c("Theme", "Quantitative finding", "Field observation", "Convergence"),
    align     = c("l", "l", "l", "c"),
    escape    = FALSE,
    caption   = "Table 4.3.  Convergence of quantitative findings and field observation across the four themes"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "bordered"),
    full_width = TRUE, font_size = 12
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "8em", color = "#1D6FA4") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "26em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "26em", italic = TRUE, color = "#555") %>%
  column_spec(4, bold = TRUE, width = "9em") %>%
  row_spec(4, background = "#F7F7F7")

```

This agreement between a regression coefficient and an informal field account deserves to be taken seriously, but not overstated. It is not independent confirmation in any rigorous sense, since the field material was never collected with the structure that would require. What it offers instead is a check against a real risk of working with data like MCHTrack’s: a coefficient can be statistically significant and still tell you very little true about the world, simply because the data behind it is thin in the wrong places. Where the regression and the field account agreed, that risk looks smaller. Where they did not, the largest regression deviations in Section III.A.iii sat in the state with the least reliable records, and the supply-side gap raised in Section IV.D sits entirely outside what either the regression or the field engagement could see at all. This thesis has tried to treat both kinds of disagreement, and both kinds of silence, with the same weight as the agreements, rather than setting them aside. A dissertation built on routine digital health records must state plainly where those records can be relied upon and where they cannot.

# V. Conclusion and Recommendations

## A. Implications by driver

This thesis asked what predicts zero-dose status and tracing effectiveness in MCHTrack. The two models answer differently. DATHARM’s two underlying problems, finding zero-dose children and getting them vaccinated once found, call for different fixes as a result.

Distance is the strongest predictor of zero-dose status. It grows far stronger once the definition narrows to children with no vaccine contact at all. Continued or expanded outreach into the wards where physical distance is greatest stands the best chance of finding children the current system is most likely to miss. The household enumeration gap raised throughout this thesis adds urgency to this. DATHARM’s own Kano coordinator estimated that roughly one in five households go unreached during enumeration. If that estimate holds, the children furthest from a facility are plausibly also the children least likely to be found at all. The population this thesis can describe statistically is probably smaller than the population that needs reaching.

Distance loses almost all of this predictive power once a child is flagged and a tracing attempt begins. SMS and phone contact do the work of recovery, not physical reach. Investment in contact infrastructure, working numbers, message delivery, is likely to do more for recovery than investment in physical reach would. This should not be applied uniformly across both states, however. SMS outperforms home visits in Katsina; the reverse holds in Kano. DATHARM’s existing practice of treating method choice as a local operational decision, rather than a fixed national protocol, already reflects the right instinct.

The clearest single recommendation in this thesis concerns recovery reporting itself. Recovery measured strictly, on confirmed in-network vaccination, sits at 22 per cent. Measured permissively, including unverified off-network care, it rises to 43 per cent. Neither figure is wrong. They answer different questions. The gap between them is large enough to change how a funder or DATHARM’s own leadership might judge the programme’s performance. Any reported recovery figure should state which definition produced it, and where possible, both figures should be reported side by side. The gap was never hidden in the data. It was only ever uncollapsed.

## B. What remains unresolved about weather, and why

Section IV.B offered five explanations for why weather shows no detectable effect on visits in this dataset, despite comparable effects found twice elsewhere. Social and operational rhythm may already absorb most of the swing in daily visits before weather can register. Conflict and administrative disruption may crowd out a gentler stressor entirely. A real response to heat may exist within a single day, shifting when a visit happens rather than whether it happens, invisible to data recorded only by date. Heat may act through labour and household time rather than through travel deterrence directly. The outcome variable itself may simply be too noisy to detect an effect that is real but small.

This thesis cannot choose between these five. The temptation to choose anyway is worth resisting on purpose. A single registry, two states, and twenty months of data are not enough to adjudicate between five mechanisms operating at different scales, the household, the day, the region. Conflict dominance is the strongest candidate by reputation, and picking it as the answer would have produced a tidier conclusion. It would also have been a false one, since nothing in this thesis actually rules out the other four. A confidently resolved null would have been easier to write and harder to defend under scrutiny. Five named, evidenced candidates attached to an honestly unresolved null describe more accurately what a single study of this kind can establish. Each one also points to a specific gap in what was measured, rather than a vague call for more research, which leaves a clearer trail for whoever tests this relationship next.

Two of the five point directly to what that next step should capture. If heat’s effect operates within a day rather than across days, MCHTrack would need a time-of-day field, not just a date, to find it. If conflict and disrupted administration crowd out weather as a demand-side shock, the same disruption plausibly affects supply. A programme blind to stockouts and missed opportunities cannot rule that out either. Both possibilities are addressed directly in the recommendations below.

## C. Limitations

Four limitations have run through this thesis and are worth gathering here. MCHTrack records children who are found, not children who exist. The household enumeration gap has no field anywhere in the system, and every zero-dose count inherits it silently. Katsina’s facility visit records carry a documented duplication problem, 38.9 per cent of records affected by a device handover, worked around in this thesis but not repaired. Recovery can be confirmed by a card check with no record of what the card showed, producing the strict-versus-permissive gap discussed above. This analysis also tested demand-side explanations only. It has no visibility into stockouts, cold-chain failures, or staffing gaps, and evidence from elsewhere in Nigeria suggests this blind spot is unlikely to be small.

A further limitation concerns what could not be measured even in principle. Household socioeconomic status, maternal education, and birth order are absent from MCHTrack’s fields entirely. The system also has no way to check whether a caregiver’s account of a vaccination history was accurate or approximate, a real source of error wherever a vaccine is identified informally rather than by name.

None of this is unique to MCHTrack. Three observations are likely to recur in any community-based digital immunisation tracking system built on a similar design. Ward-level analysis built on this kind of data tends to look most informative exactly where the underlying records are least reliable. Any system allowing a case to close on an unverified confirmation step will generate a gap between what it reports and what it can prove. A system built around demand-side identification will, by construction, be blind to supply-side failure. The three describe the same underlying risk from different angles. A system can look more trustworthy than it is, through a dramatic statistic, a clean-looking recovery rate, or a quiet stretch of records. In each case, the very gap that should raise suspicion is what produces the reassuring appearance in the first place. Organisations running similar programmes elsewhere may find these three questions useful to ask of their own data before treating any of the three appearances at face value.

The specific numbers in this thesis belong to Kano and Katsina in this period. The coefficients, the percentages, the reversal between two states, none of it is claimed to travel further than that.

## D. Future research directions

Three directions extend beyond this thesis’s specific dataset and setting.

The first concerns whether weather affects immunisation-seeking behaviour in this regional context at all. Answering that question properly requires a design built to test it directly, rather than infer it from data collected for another purpose. Twenty months of data across two states cannot separate the five explanations raised in Section V.B from one another, and cannot rule out that a longer, wider dataset would detect an effect this one was simply not positioned to see. A study spanning several years rather than twenty months would let weather variation move independently of any single conflict episode or single religious calendar cycle, rather than being confounded with whatever happened to coincide with this particular window. Coverage across more states, or a comparable registry spanning a wider footprint of the Sahel, would give a design enough range to compare high-conflict against low-conflict wards, or agricultural-peak against dry-season periods, with the statistical power this thesis’s sample could not support. Most importantly, such a study would need to measure the channels this thesis could only name. A time-of-day field would test whether heat shifts visit timing rather than presence. A ward-level conflict-exposure measure would test whether instability crowds out weather sensitivity. A seasonal labour-calendar variable would test the labour-capacity account directly. Even a simple stockout indicator would test whether a null result reflects unmeasured supply failure rather than the absence of a true weather effect.

The second concerns whether heat affects preventive and curative care-seeking differently. The existing literature on heat and healthcare utilisation is large, but concentrated almost entirely on illness-driven demand. Heat has been linked repeatedly to increased hospital admissions for dehydration, cardiovascular events, and respiratory conditions across high-income settings. Siddiqi et al. and Samano et al. remain the rare exceptions testing heat against scheduled rather than illness-driven care, and they reach different conclusions from each other and from this thesis. Whether that divergence reflects setting, care type, or simply underpowered data in at least one of the three studies is not yet answerable, and a deliberately designed comparison would be needed before treating any one of the three findings as more representative than another.

The third concerns how digital immunisation registries perform across different national contexts, and recent work already provides a template rather than an open question. Mantel et al. (2025) evaluated electronic immunisation registries and logistics systems across Guinea, Honduras, Rwanda, and Tanzania, finding substantial variation in data accuracy and user experience between countries, and documented their methodology specifically so it could be replicated elsewhere. No conflict-affected or Sahelian country was included in that sample. Applying the same evaluation framework to MCHTrack and comparable systems in Nigeria and the wider Sahel would test directly whether the limitations identified in this thesis, the enumeration gap, the verification gap, the supply-side blind spot, are general features of this kind of system or specific to the setting examined here.

MCHTrack was built to find children the health system was missing. This thesis set out to do the same to the data itself, and to the question of weather riding alongside it. The aim was to find where the record can be trusted, where it cannot, and where the answer is still genuinely unknown. A record is not the same as the life it tries to follow. A null result is not the same as an absence. The distance between what was found and what remains unresolved is where the real work of reaching every child will always have to continue.
